lesson.title: Shaking Hands Before You Talk
lesson.summary: A connection oriented service model requires two endpoints to establish shared state before exchanging data and to formally close that state afterward, trading a small amount of setup delay for the ability to track a coherent session, as TCP does with its handshake and teardown.
lesson.body:
A connection oriented service model is one in which the two communicating endpoints first establish a connection, meaning they agree on and store some shared state about the conversation, before any application data is exchanged, and they formally tear down that state when the conversation ends. This is one of the two fundamental service models a transport layer protocol can offer, the other being connectionless, and the choice between them is one of the most consequential decisions in how a protocol behaves.

TCP is the internet's primary connection oriented transport protocol, and its three way handshake is the canonical example of connection establishment. The client sends a SYN segment proposing an initial sequence number, the server responds with a SYN ACK segment acknowledging that number and proposing its own, and the client responds with an ACK segment confirming the server's number. Only after this three segment exchange completes do the two sides consider the connection established and begin sending actual application data. Closing a TCP connection is similarly explicit, typically involving an exchange of FIN and ACK segments from each side, so that both endpoints agree the conversation has ended before either discards its state.

It is worth being precise that connection oriented describes the presence of established, tracked session state, and is not automatically the same thing as reliable delivery, even though TCP happens to bundle both together. A connection oriented protocol could in principle establish a session and still not guarantee that every piece of data arrives, though in practice the connection state that a handshake establishes, tracking sequence numbers and acknowledgments, is exactly the bookkeeping that makes reliable delivery possible, which is why the two concepts are so often paired and why reliable delivery is covered as a natural extension of connection oriented service.

A phone call is a helpful everyday analogy. Before either party says anything meaningful, the caller dials, the phone rings, and the other person answers, at which point both sides confirm the connection with a greeting. Only then does the actual conversation happen, and when it is over, both parties typically say goodbye and hang up, explicitly ending the call rather than one side simply walking away. Compare this to dropping a postcard in a mailbox, where there is no ringing, no confirmation of receipt, and no formal goodbye, which is the connectionless model covered next.

The cost of this handshake is latency. Establishing a TCP connection takes at least one full round trip before any application data can even be sent, and if the connection also needs TLS encryption negotiated on top, that adds further round trips before the first useful byte moves. For a single short request, such as a DNS lookup, this setup cost can dominate the total time, which is exactly why some transport layer protocols deliberately avoid connection establishment altogether, accepting the tradeoffs of a connectionless service model instead.
